title: THE HISTORY OF SNICKERS — THE CANDY BAR NAMED AFTER A DEAD HORSE
fullText: The bestselling chocolate bar in the world is named after a horse that died several months before the bar itself was even created. It's a touching detail. Now for the less touching part. The company behind it was built on a family feud so bitter that the father personally forced his own son out of the business, handed him $50,000 in severance, and reportedly told him, "There's not enough room in this company for both of us. Go to another country and start your own." The son left and built a competing chocolate empire on the other side of the Atlantic. One that decades later would acquire his father's company, closing the circle right where it had all begun. The family behind Snickers has remained remarkably private. One of its patriarchs gave what appears to have been his only interview, decided afterward that he's been misqued, and never spoke publicly again for the rest of his life. I'll tell you how a chocolate bar created as a tribute to a beloved family horse became the bestselling candy bar in history through a father and son feud, a secretive European empire, and an almost obsessive commitment to privacy that still defines one of the largest privately held companies in the world. The story begins in 1911 when Frank Mars founded the Marobar Company in Minnesota after several unsuccessful attempts to establish himself in the confectionary business. His real breakthrough came in 1923 with the Milky Way Bar, which finally brought the company serious money and allowed production to move to Chicago. Riding that success, Frank and his second wife, Ethel, purchased [music] nearly 3,000 acres of land in Tennessee and established a farm they jokingly called Milky Way Farm after the very candy bar that had made the family wealthy. There they raised pedigreed herford cattle and thoroughbred raceh horses. One of those horses, a favorite of the entire family, was named Snickers. There's an almost amusing detail here that few people ever think about. Naming the farm after one candy bar and then giving the name of a beloved horse from that same farm to the next candy bar looks like a small personal ritual for a family whose business and everyday life had been intertwined from the very beginning with almost no boundary between work and home. Meanwhile, [music] the company was developing a new product. Peanut-based nougat, caramel, and roasted peanuts covered in milk chocolate. A recipe inspired by an existing street confection that they essentially decided to put inside a chocolate coating. The product didn't even have a name yet. The team was still debating the formula and packaging when the horse named Snickers suddenly died. The family decided to preserve the memory of their beloved animal by giving its name to the new product. A touching but essentially accidental choice that would define the brand's identity for nearly a century. The bar hit the market in 1930 and immediately caused a scandal of a very different kind. It cost 20 while the standard price for a chocolate bar at the time was only 5. Production was still almost entirely done by hand. Workers poured the peanut nougat into molds, layered the caramel and peanuts, cut each bar by hand, and dipped them one by one into melted chocolate. Despite costing four times the market price, the bar caught on and eventually became the bestselling candy bar in history, surpassing even the Milky Way that had once saved the family business from bankruptcy. What's interesting is that the recipe has barely changed since then. The same four layers, nubat, caramel, roasted peanuts, and milk chocolate that it had nearly a century ago. Today, producing the enormous daily volume of bars requires around 100 tons of peanuts with each individual bar containing an average of roughly 16 peanuts. A rare case where a century old mass market recipe has remained virtually untouched while everything around it has changed. The packaging, the advertising, and even the name used on different continents. And this is where the story gets genuinely interesting, the part the company never includes in its official press releases. Frank's son, Forest Mars, joined the family business in 1929 after graduating from Yale University with a degree in industrial engineering. He proved to be a talented engineer, helping his father optimize production processes and eliminate inefficiencies left over from the company's early almost artisal beginnings. But Forest had much more ambitious plans. He wanted to expand the business beyond the United States, starting with Canada, and demanded a third of the company in exchange for leading the expansion. Frank refused. The conversation escalated into an open conflict that ended with the father giving his son a choice. Stay under the existing conditions or leave altogether. Forest chose to leave or according to some versions gave his father the ultimatum himself, declaring that he would walk away unless he received a stake immediately. [music] Frank eventually handed his son $50,000 and the rights to manufacture Milky Way overseas, effectively pushing him out of the family business with the message that there wasn't enough room in the company for both of them. It's important to understand the scale of the break in the context of the era. The 1930s were just beginning. The Great Depression had already engulfed the country. And for a young man without a guaranteed place in the family business, leaving meant a real, not merely symbolic risk of ending up with nothing. $50,000 was a substantial sum for the time, but it was hardly a guarantee of success on another continent where Forest had neither connections nor established production facilities nor a recognizable name. Forest didn't simply survive being pushed out. He built a parallel empire that would eventually become even larger than his father's. After moving to the English town of slow, he founded his own company and in 1932 introduced the Mars Bar, essentially a reworked version of his father's Milky Way, adapted to British tastes, sweeter nougat, different caramel proportions, and packaging designed specifically for European consumers who were still unfamiliar with Americanstyle chocolate bars. In 1936, Malteses followed. Forest also moved into Pet Food, founding Pedigree Pet Foods, a business division that decades later would become one of the corporation's major sources of revenue, at one point even surpassing chocolate sales. Forest worked in his new home with the same obsession as his father, only multiplied by a frugality bordering on the extreme. He was so miserly with personal expenses that his father-in-law once deliberately sailed to England to bring Forest's wife Audrey and their young children back to the United States. Unable to tolerate [music] the conditions in which he believed his daughter's family was living. Publicity was never one of Forest's strengths. From the very beginning, he preferred to conduct business quietly and away from the spotlight. long before that trait would become a defining characteristic of the entire family for the next h 100red years. In 1941, after returning to the United States at the outbreak of World War II, Forest partnered with another businessman to create M&M's. While in a separate joint venture with a Texas entrepreneur, he helped create the Uncle Ben's rice brand. One revealing detail about his character when the US military asked him during the war to share patents for quick cooking rice technology with other manufacturers so production could be expanded for the armed forces. Forest refused and the war ended before anyone could force him to reveal the manufacturing secrets to competitors. For him, apparently, business remained business, even in the middle of a global conflict, and commercial secrecy mattered more than patriotic appeals to share technology for the common wartime effort. Frank Mars died of a heart attack in 1934, and the Chicago business passed on through inheritance, but not to the exiled forest. Instead, it went to other relatives and minority shareholders, including Forest's halfsister. For the next 30 years, the two Mars companies, American and European, operated in parallel, formally belonging to the same family, but being managed completely separately with different recipes, different packaging, and even different names for similar products. That was when a strange quirk emerged that can still be found on British storeshelves today. The bar known in Britain as Mars Bar is called Milky Way in America. While what Britain's call Milky Way tastes much closer to the American Three Musketeers, a product that essentially doesn't exist outside the United States. The split within a single family literally became embedded in the different names given to similar candy bars on opposite sides of the Atlantic. It wasn't until 1964 that Forest finally bought out the remaining shareholders of the American business, including his halfsister, Patricia, and merged his British Food Manufacturers Inc. with his father's Chicago company into a single organization called Mars Incorporated. With roughly 80% of the company still remaining in family hands, after taking control of the newly unified company, he immediately began implementing the principles of rigorous scientific management he had developed through his engineering education. strict quality control, a flat organizational structure without unnecessary offices, and the famous practice of having even senior executives work at ordinary desks in a shared open plan space. Highly unusual for corporate America in the midentth century, 30 years after his father had personally thrown him out of the business, Forest didn't simply return. He became the man who reunited both halves of the family legacy under one roof and took over the resulting company as president and chief executive. From that moment on, the word Mars on a package began to represent a global corporation rather than one of two competing branches of the same family. Forest's management style after the merger shaped the company's culture for decades, and that culture was built around an almost pathological level of privacy. In 1966, Forest gave the only interview of his entire life to the trade publication Candy Industry. After feeling that he had been misqued, he vowed never to speak publicly to the press again and kept that promise until his death in 1999. He raised his three children, Forest Jr., John, and Jacqueline, by the same rules. Avoid journalists, distrust outsiders, and never discuss the family's wealth publicly. Jacqueline once reportedly walked out of a lunch after discovering that she had been seated next to the publisher of Forbes simply because the magazine had dared to include the family on its list of the world's wealthiest people. Today, Mars Incorporated remains one of the largest privately held companies in the United States with annual revenue in the tens of billions of dollars. Yet almost nobody outside the industry could identify a current member of the Mars family by sight. Even later generations of the family, including Victoria Mars, Forest Senior's granddaughter, who became chair of the board in 2014, have generally stayed away from the public spotlight despite her Yale degree and MBA from Wharton. Paradoxically, that very secrecy fueled journalists fascination for the family for decades more than openness ever could have. The less information the Mars family provided about themselves, the more reporters tried to figure out what was hidden behind the silence. From the true details of the family split in the 1930s to the actual scale of a fortune the family itself never publicly confirmed or denied. In later decades, the next generation, Forest Jr. and John, who eventually ran the company together, inherited not only the family fortune, but also their father's tendency toward internal conflict. Their own rivalry over control of the business occasionally created considerable turmoil inside a company whose corporate culture had once been built around the principle of egalitarianism. There's also a much more harmless, almost comical chapter in the brand's history, directly connected to the legacy of that split between the American and European branches of the company. From 1968 to 1990, the bar known to the rest of the world as Snickers was sold in the United Kingdom and Ireland under a completely different name, Marathon. The reason went back to the separate histories of the two companies. The British product line had developed independently from the American business and acquired its own local name which remained in use for more than two decades. In 1990, as part of a global effort to standardize the brands after the businesses had been reunited, Mars decided to bring the name [music] into line with the rest of the world and renamed Marathon Snickers throughout the United Kingdom and Ireland. The official explanation was straightforward. In the United States, the company had briefly sold a completely different product under the name Marathon during the 1970s. And having the same name referred to different products in different markets created unnecessary confusion for international travelers and complicated the brand's logistics. Consumer reaction turned out to be far less enthusiastic than the company had expected. The bar, which had been the bestselling chocolate bar in Britain before the renaming, fell to third place after the change. Some customers deliberately boycotted the product simply because the name had changed, a peculiar echo of the same stubborn sense of identity and pride that had shaped the company behind the bar for decades. Even today, more than 30 years after the rebranding, older British consumers will occasionally walk into a shop and ask for a marathon out of Hudit, despite the fact that the product hasn't been sold under that name for longer than it ever was in the first place. By 2009, the brand faced a much more serious problem than its name. Sales in the United States were declining, while its marketing messages varied dramatically from country to country. In some markets, Snickers was positioned as a manly bar for active young men. Elsewhere, it was simply treated as an ordinary snack with no single idea connecting the campaigns. Snickers risked losing its position as the world's bestselling chocolate bar precisely when competitors were beginning to close the gap on storeshelves. The solution came from the advertising agency BBDO, a universal human truth that could work in virtually any culture without translation. When people are hungry, they become completely different versions of themselves, usually irritated, irrational, or difficult to deal with. And a Snickers brings them back to normal. The idea was deliberately simple because the brand's biggest problem in previous years had been an excess of complicated, highly localized advertising concepts that didn't travel well from one market to another. The campaign's debut came during the 2010 Super Bowl. In the first commercial, 88-year-old actress Betty White plays American backyard [music] football, clumsily falls into the mud, and snaps at her teammates until one player's girlfriend hands her a Snickers. After taking a bite, White literally transforms back into a young man named Mike, whom everyone had been addressing before the transformation. The production crew later spoke admirably of White. Despite her age, she insisted on performing some of the physical falls herself rather than relying entirely on a stunt double. [music] The commercial became a genuine sensation. It topped USA Today's annual ranking of the best Super Bowl commercials, put Betty White back at the center of popular culture for weeks, and was even referenced in an episode of The Office. During the first year after the campaign launched, global brand sales increased by nearly 16%, while over 2 years, the campaign generated an additional $376 million in revenue. The increase was so widespread that marketing teams in 56 [music] of the brand's 58 markets reported gains in market share. An unusually consistent result for a campaign designed to be locally adapted rather than simply using one identical commercial everywhere. The slogan, you're not you when you're hungry, has since been used [music] across 56 of those 58 markets, repeatedly refreshed with new celebrities from Elton John to Robin Williams and William Defoe, while always preserving the same simple premise. Hunger turns you into someone else. The company eventually pushed the [music] idea beyond traditional advertising with Hungarithm, an algorithm that monitored the level of [music] irritation in American social media posts in real time and automatically lowered the price of a Snickers bar in participating stores when online hangry aggression reached particularly high levels. It was an unexpected technological extension of a remarkably simple advertising idea that had first appeared almost 15 years earlier. Let's return to where we started. The beloved horse of a family that died shortly before its name became permanently attached to the bestselling chocolate bar in history. The company built around that touching tribute spent the next 90 years doing little but surviving splits and reunifications. A father forced his son out with $50,000. The son built a parallel empire on the other side of the Atlantic and 30 years later that same son returned and reunited both halves under one roof. The family that emerged from that conflict chose absolute privacy for itself, a lifetime of silence, a refusal to speak to the press, even a dramatic walk out from a lunch simply because a Forbes journalist was sitting nearby. And yet they built [music] a brand whose most successful advertising campaign rests on almost the opposite idea. That every one of us occasionally becomes someone else, less pleasant and less recognizable. And that one simple human act can bring us back to ourselves. Perhaps that is the most subtle irony in the entire history of Snickers. A family that spent generations refusing to speak openly or honestly about itself created a brand whose central idea is almost the exact opposite. Be honest with yourself. Admit that you're not quite yourself right now and do something simple to fix it. A company built on a father and son rapture now sells the idea of reconnecting with your normal self through a chocolate bar rather than the difficult conversation the Mars family itself carefully avoided for three generations. If you enjoyed this story, subscribe. There's more to come. And here's the question for the comments. What surprised you more? that the bar was named after a horse or that an entire corporate empire grew out of a father's ultimatum go to another country. Personally, the hardest part for me to write was Forest's silence after that one interview. It's rare to find someone who decided never to speak to the press again and kept that promise literally until the final day of his life, [music] despite decades of curiosity from the rest of the world.
